title: anyone who turns a light on
hookLine: a boy tells the truth at a teacher's door; why Hindus honor the guru

cards: A boy named Satyakama wants to study with a teacher, and a student was expected to name his family line. So he asks his mother.
She tells him the truth: when she was young she worked as a servant, going from place to place, and she doesn't know his line. All she knows is that her name is Jabala and his is Satyakama.
So he walks to the teacher Gautama and repeats it, word for word. The teacher's answer: only a true brahmin would speak like that. Go and fetch the firewood.
I'll teach you, because you didn't stray from the truth.

teach.h: GU — DARKNESS, RU — WHAT REMOVES IT
teach.b: Guru. A teacher, but in Hinduism much more than a teacher of facts: the one who helps you see. A later text plays with the sound: gu is darkness, and ru is what removes it.
Wordplay, but a vivid one. Watch what Satyakama's teacher does next. He hands the boy four hundred thin, weak cows to look after, and Satyakama says he won't come back until they're a thousand.
Years pass in the forest. On the way home he's taught by a bull, a fire, a swan and a diving bird. He arrives glowing, and his teacher says: your face shines like someone who knows.
But Satyakama asks him to teach him anyway.
Learning that comes from a teacher, he says, is the kind that turns out best. That's how Hinduism holds the guru: not a salesman with a course, but the one who lifts the dark.
An old charge to students says it plainly: treat your mother as God, your father as God, your teacher as God.

It's why many students of Indian music and dance touch their teacher's feet before they perform, why learning passes down a long line of teachers, and why, on the full moon called Guru Purnima, students thank their gurus.
For some Hindus, God is the first guru, or the guru within. Either way, the light came from somewhere.

how: Hindus may learn from a guru within a lineage (parampara), receive instruction or a mantra from them, and honor teachers on Guru Purnima; in some traditions, God is understood as the first or inner guru.

games.q: dance recital tonight!! before i went on i touched my dance teacher's feet and Sam asked if that's like… worshipping her? 😳
o: it's how we honor a guru, the one who lifts the dark. the old line says treat your teacher as God. even Satyakama, after a bull and a fire taught him, still wanted his teacher.
yes, she's basically a goddess to us.
it's just for luck, like knocking on wood.
games.why: Satyakama's teacher took him in and taught him, and Satyakama came back to learn more. Hindus honor the guru almost like God, so a student bows to the teacher.

games.q: match the story to the word.
p: told the truth about his family
the teacher who took him in
a full-moon day to thank teachers

s: the teacher turned Satyakama away for not knowing his family line
he took him in because he told the truth.
Satyakama asked his teacher to teach him, even after a bull, a fire and two birds had
he said learning from a teacher is the kind that turns out best.

the guru is the one who helps you see: who removes the dark.

games.q: you're Satyakama at the teacher's door. you don't know your family line, and the other students know theirs. what do you say?
o: say exactly what your mother told you.
games.why: Gautama took him in for it: you didn't stray from the truth. fetch the firewood. a guru looks for an honest student.

practice: Today, remember one light. Rest your hands in your lap, or bring your palms together the way students greet a teacher. Bring to mind one person who helped you see: a teacher, a grandparent, a coach, a friend with one true sentence.
Let their face come. Then, silently, thank them. If you pray, thank God for them too.
If you like, bow your head a little, the way a student does. The bell holds the time.

wordCard.voice: Guru. A teacher who helps you see; in one Upanishad's play on the sound, the one who removes the dark. Twelfth word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: teacher. One Upanishad reads it as gu, darkness, and ru, what stops it.

carryVoice: Your line: thank a teacher today. In Hinduism a guru is honored almost like God; a two-line message to yours is a good start. Day twelve.

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 4.4–4.9 (Satyakama Jabala: truthfulness, the herd, teachings from bull, fire, swan and diving bird; 4.9.3 learning from a teacher)
